title: The snapshot stores the entry and its last error; retry state is recomputed on restore, and hopeless items expire
context: Deciding what reaches the disk forces a distinction the in-memory queue is allowed to leave vague. `flushFailed` encodes two different facts into one field: `nextAttemptAt: null` means either that the backoff budget is spent — a 5xx that may well succeed later — or that the failure is not retryable at all. While the queue lives only in memory and the recorder is looking at the row, that conflation costs nothing, because a human decides whether to press retry. Once the queue is restored and resent automatically, the two have to be told apart: a 401 is a session that expired and everything queued behind it should go out the moment the user signs in again, while a 404 for a game somebody deleted can never succeed and should not cost a doomed request on every launch. There is a second consequence of writing the queue down that is easy to miss. Today the only way out of the queue for a permanently failing entry is closing the app; the queue is memory. Persisting it removes that escape hatch, so a stuck entry becomes stuck forever — the indicator reads unsynced for that game indefinitely, and under D3 the user cannot even see it once they leave the game.
decision: One key, `pending-writes`, holding `{ version, items: [{ entry, gameId, setIndex, lastError?, firstFailedAt? }] }` written as a whole snapshot on every queue change. The version lives in the snapshot and not in the key: a versioned key would be a second copy of the same number, and a build that bumped it would look elsewhere entirely, leaving the old snapshot unread and undiscarded. `lastError` carries `{ code, reason, status }` from `ApiClientError` and nothing else — `detail` and `message` are human-facing strings that move with copy changes and i18n. `firstFailedAt` is set once, on the first failure, because a flush re-sends every pending entry for its game and a timestamp that moved with each attempt would measure the recorder's activity rather than the entry's age. `attempts` and `nextAttemptAt` are not stored but recomputed on restore, and `flushingGameIds` is runtime state that is false by construction after a restart. A `version` that does not match causes the whole snapshot to be ignored rather than migrated, and the store is cleared only when that version is one this build has already moved past — a newer one may belong to a build the user is also running, and that is the one guess here that destroys unsent work. Whether another attempt is worth making is decided in exactly one place, the threshold the flush already applies, and the flush, the restore and the expiry rule all read it — there is no second predicate and no table mapping codes to policy. Against the lost escape hatch, restore applies a narrowed expiry: an entry whose last failure is worth retrying never expires, and one whose last failure is not is dropped after seven days.

alternatives.option: Store a `retryable` boolean instead of the error code
alternatives.reason: Smaller, but it collapses 401 and 400 into the same value while their correct handling is opposite: one should go out again after the user signs in, the other can never succeed. It also leaves `offline-recording` nothing to key its conflict flow on.

alternatives.option: Store nothing about the failure and reset every restored item to attempt immediately
alternatives.reason: Simplest, and it changes nothing about the shape of `PendingEntry`. But an entry for a deleted game then costs one doomed request on every single app launch and keeps the queue permanently non-empty with no way to tell it apart from work that might still succeed.

Preserves the schedule exactly, which sounds faithful but is wrong on both counts: a stored absolute timestamp is always in the past after a restart, and an item whose backoff was spent stays dead — invisible under D3, so nothing will ever attempt it again.

alternatives.option: Migrate old snapshots when the shape changes instead of discarding them
alternatives.reason: A migration path is worth writing when the data is irreplaceable and long-lived. This queue holds seconds to hours of unsent work in the normal case, and a migration bug would corrupt exactly the data the Change exists to protect.

alternatives.option: Give the user an explicit discard gesture on the failed row instead of an expiry
alternatives.reason: The semantically correct answer, and where this should eventually land. But a discard the user cannot see is not a discard, and making unsent work visible outside the recording screen is `offline-recording`'s criterion, not this Change's.

alternatives.option: Expire every item after seven days, retryable or not
alternatives.reason: One rule instead of two, but it deletes work that could still succeed — a week-long tournament with no signal is the case that most needs the queue to hold, and it is exactly the case this would break.

alternatives.option: Widen the restore's question so an expired session is retried on the next start
alternatives.reason: Attractive because signing in leaves the app and returns as a fresh start, so a restart is often what fixed it. But it introduces a second standard that disagrees with the flush's over exactly one status, and every later reader has to hold both. What it buys is narrow: nothing is sent until the recorder opens that game anyway, and when they do the indicator shows the queue unsynced and the retry gesture is already there. One standard, plus a gesture that already exists, beats two standards.

consequences: `PendingEntry` gains `lastError` and `firstFailedAt`. Both are justified by serialisation rather than by the in-memory model needing them: the failure reason was already reaching `flushFailed` and being encoded into `nextAttemptAt` on arrival, and the age has no meaning until the queue outlives the process.

An expired session is not resent automatically after a restart. It stays queued and the indicator reports it, and the recorder's existing retry gesture sends it once they have signed back in — which is the same gesture that already covers every other failure they can see.

Restore behaviour has a data-loss path by construction: an entry whose failure is not worth retrying silently disappears after seven days. Seven days has no measured basis; it is chosen to restore the property persistence removed, not because the number means anything.

The expiry rule becomes the primary mechanism rather than a safety net once request validation lands on the rally endpoint and 400s become common. Because an entry is enqueued and written to disk before any request is sent, boundary validation cannot keep malformed entries out of the queue — it can only increase how many get stuck in it.
The threshold has one home, so the flush, the restore and the expiry rule cannot drift apart.
revisitTriggers: `offline-recording` makes unsent work visible outside the recording screen: an explicit discard becomes possible and should replace the expiry rather than sit alongside it.
Request validation lands on the rally endpoint: 400s stop being rare, and the seven-day rule moves from insurance to the main path, which is the point at which its value deserves measurement.
A tournament longer than the expiry window is recorded offline, or the field shows entries expiring that should not have.

Anything else needs to know why a write failed — error reporting, a per-row explanation, the conflict flow — at which point the fields stored here should be reconsidered against that consumer rather than kept minimal by default.
